title: Cartesian coordinates in two dimensions
summary: Read, plot and transform points in four quadrants, then use coordinate differences to solve geometric problems.
objectives: Read and interpret ordered pairs in all four quadrants.
Use coordinates to describe translations, reflections and midpoints.
Find horizontal and vertical lengths, perimeters and areas from coordinates.

sections.title: Read an ordered pair from the axes

blocks.text: An ordered pair is written (x, y). Start at the origin, move horizontally to the x-coordinate, and then move vertically to the y-coordinate. Reversing the order usually names a different point. A point on the x-axis has y = 0, a point on the y-axis has x = 0, and the origin is (0, 0).

The quadrant sign pattern is a check, not a replacement for reading the scales. First identify the value represented by one grid interval, especially when an axis is marked in twos, halves or another scale.

sections.title: Describe movement and reflection with coordinates

blocks.text: A translation adds the same horizontal and vertical changes to every point. Moving h units right and k units up maps (x, y) to (x + h, y + k); a negative value means left or down. The shape, size and orientation stay unchanged.

A reflection changes the coordinate perpendicular to the mirror line. In the x-axis, y changes sign: (x, y) becomes (x, -y). In the y-axis, x changes sign: (x, y) becomes (-x, y). A point on the mirror line remains fixed. In the diagram, A and A-prime have opposite x-coordinates and the same y-coordinate.

For a horizontal segment, subtract the x-coordinates and use the positive distance. For a vertical segment, subtract the y-coordinates. These distances can be combined to find the perimeter and area of an axis-aligned rectangle.

The midpoint is halfway in both directions, so average the x-coordinates and average the y-coordinates. Keep brackets around negative values before adding. A quick check is that the midpoint must lie between the two endpoint coordinates on each axis.

sections.title: Worked example: rectangle from four coordinates

prompt.text: A rectangle has vertices (-3, 4), (5, 4), (5, -2) and (-3, -2). Find its perimeter and area.

content.text: Find the horizontal side using the two x-values.
Find the vertical side using the two y-values.
Use the perimeter and area formulas.

sections.verification_note: Opposite sides have equal coordinate differences; 8 + 6 + 8 + 6 = 28, and an 8-by-6 rectangle has area 48.

sections.title: Worked example: translate, reflect and find a midpoint

prompt.text: Point P(-5, 2) is translated 7 units right and 3 units down to Q. Q is then reflected in the x-axis to R. Find Q, R and the midpoint of QR.

content.text: Add 7 to x and subtract 3 from y.
Reflection in the x-axis keeps x and reverses the sign of y.
Average corresponding coordinates for the midpoint.

sections.verification_note: Q and R are one unit below and above the x-axis, so their midpoint (2, 0) lies on the mirror line.

prompt.text: Point A(-4, 7) is reflected in the y-axis. State the x-coordinate of its image.

feedback.text: Reflection in the y-axis changes -4 to 4 and keeps the y-coordinate unchanged.

blocks.text: Read x before y and check the quadrant signs against the axis scales. For translations, add the stated movement; for reflections, change only the coordinate perpendicular to the mirror axis.
Use absolute coordinate differences for horizontal and vertical lengths. Average matching coordinates for a midpoint, then check that the result lies halfway between the endpoints.
